facts.claim: "I Love You" was released on 17 February 2022 as the second single from Skinty Fia. The album came out on 22 April 2022 and Dan Carey produced it.

Skinty Fia was released through Partisan Records. Dan Carey is credited as producer and mixer, and he also played synths and the Swarmatron and did sonic manipulation. The album was recorded at Angelic Studios and mastered at Abbey Road Studios.
The album's band lineup is Conor Deegan III on bass, Tom Coll on drums and percussion, and Carlos O'Connell and Conor Curley on guitars. Grian Chatten is credited with the words on most tracks.
Skinty Fia was recorded in 2021 in London with Dan Carey, who also produced the band's first two albums, Dogrel and A Hero's Death.

Chatten called "I Love You" the first overtly political song the band had written. He said he wanted to take an ostensibly cliché title and topic and make it his own, and it turned out to be another song about Ireland.
Chatten said he had moved away from Ireland, now lives in a country responsible for much of Ireland's chaos, and feels guilty for having left.
The song refers to the 2017 discovery of the remains of 800 children at a former mother and baby home in Ireland.

Songfacts reports that the song came out of a jam session. Drummer Tom Coll stopped playing to collect a Deliveroo order, the three guitars kept going, and Chatten began his rant with no drums behind him.
The video was directed by Sam Taylor. In it, Chatten walks through a candle-lit church, calmly for the first half of the song and with more anger in the second half.
A year after the album's release, the band still closed every show with "I Love You", which Chatten sees as a grounding finale of hope.

research.lineage: Fontaines D.C. are a Dublin-formed Irish post-punk band whose third album, Skinty Fia, explores Irish identity and the experience of Irishness in England.

draft:
The trick of **I Love You** is that it keeps its title honest for longer than you expect. For two verses it plays as a straight devotional, the kind of pledge that reaches past the grave, and only when the language curdles do you realise who it's addressed to. Grian Chatten has said he wanted to take a cliché title and topic and make it his own, and that it turned out to be another song about Ireland. He also called it the first overtly political song Fontaines D.C. had written.

The love is real, and that's what makes the rest hurt. Chatten has said he left Ireland, now lives in a country responsible for much of its chaos, and feels guilty for going. You can hear that guilt in the shape of the lyric. The narrator who swears devotion is the same one who admits he clambered up, did what was demanded, and kept the spoils for himself. Pride and shame share a verse and never settle. Then comes the line that drops the mask: "this island's run by sharks with children's bones stuck in their jaws." It points at the 2017 discovery of the remains of 800 children at a former mother and baby home, and it lands with no metaphor to soften it. Later, the love song comes back sour and funny at once: "I loved you like a penny loves the pocket of a priest." Affection and accusation fused into one simile.

The music holds steady while the words get louder. A clean electric guitar picks arpeggios over a walking bass line and a drum kit with a firm snare, and the groove sits at a moderate, driving pace. A second, distorted guitar holds long notes behind it. The room sound is natural and close, and the voice is mostly single-tracked: mid-range, a little raw, half sung and half spoken, closer to a man talking at you than performing. That restraint is the point. The band doesn't swell to meet the anger; it lets the anger carry itself.

The song grew out of a jam. Drummer Tom Coll stepped away to collect a Deliveroo order, the three guitars kept going, and Chatten started his rant with no drums behind him. That accident shows in the finished track, where the rant sections feel like something spilling over rather than something composed. Dan Carey, who produced the band's first two records too, made Skinty Fia with them in London in 2021, at Angelic Studios. It's Irish post-punk, still angry, but turned toward grief for a home you can't stop loving and can't stand to live in.

The band still closes every show with it, and Chatten calls it a finale of hope, which tells you how he hears the anger. It's a love song that won't let love off the hook. By the last "the bastard walks by," you understand you can rage at a place precisely because you can't let it go.
